1:
The seventh month opens not with the ring of hammers on the wall but with the gathering of a whole people to hear the word of God, and the witnesses set the scene with care. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch survey these chapters as one connected whole, acts of worship led by Ezra and the priests and Levites, with Nehemiah the secular governor named only twice; the seventh month opened with the feast of trumpets and held within it both the feast of tabernacles and the great day of atonement, and at the congregation's own request Ezra read to the assembled people out of the book of the law. The reformed John Gill hears in the gathering "as one man" a great unanimity, zeal, and affection, the people crowding into a broad and commodious street that led to the water gate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers over every circumstance of the assembly. The time was the first day of the seventh month, the feast of trumpets and a holy convocation appointed in Lev. 23:24 and Num. 29:1; and it was on that day, he adds, that the altar had been set up and the burnt-offerings first renewed after the return from captivity, a fresh mercy that made the feast the more affecting. The place was the street before the water gate, spacious enough to hold the multitude the temple court could not; for though sacrifices belonged only to the temple door, praying and praising and preaching are as acceptably performed in one place as another. The persons were all the people, not compelled but voluntarily met as one man — men, women, and the children old enough to understand — and Henry presses the duty that masters of families should bring their households to the public worship of God, since women and little ones have souls to save. Ezra presided, fit above all to expound as a ready scribe in the law of his God; his call was clear, for the people themselves asked him to bring the book, so that God gave the ability and the people the opportunity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke locates the spot precisely — the water gate led from the temple down to the brook Kidron. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the emphasis of the phrase "as one man," where it is the unanimity and not the number that is stressed, and notes that Ezra, absent through the earlier chapters, now reappears for the first time in the book, having probably been at the Persian court for some twelve years.
2:
Ezra brings the long-neglected book into the open air before the congregation, and the witnesses attend to both the copy and the hearers. The reformed John Gill notes that Ezra brought forth a perfect and well-known copy of the law, fetched either from his own chest or from the temple where it was laid up, and produced it in the sight of the whole assembly, though some would restrict what he read to the book of Deuteronomy. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the reading itself: Ezra read "from the light," from early morning until midday, some six hours, yet not without pause, for the reading went on alternately with instructive lectures on the law from the Levites, while the ears of all the people were directed attentively to it.

The phrase "all that could hear with understanding" draws the witnesses to define the congregation. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes it of men, women, and children who had reached years of discretion, and marks the fitness of the day — the seventh being the most important month in a religious sense, and its first day, the feast of trumpets, the most important new moon of the year, appointed in Lev. 23:24. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same clause more strictly, excluding infants and those not likely to receive instruction; yet he turns at once to a pastoral tenderness, insisting that rather than a poor mother be deprived of the ordinances of God she should be free to come with her child in her arms, for it is cruel to shut her out on that account. He notes too that this first day of the seventh month was the opening of the civil year, ushered in by the sound of trumpets.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley joins the others in fixing the day as the feast of trumpets, called a sabbath and kept as a holy convocation by the command of Lev. 23:24, and recalls with them that it was on this very day, after the return from captivity, that the altar had been set up — a remembrance which, he thinks, had led the people to keep the feast ever since with more than ordinary solemnity. The witnesses do not divide; they gather around the single picture of a governor and scribe bringing the sacred book before a congregation that had come, women and children with the men, to hear it read and expounded from morning until noon.
3:
From daylight until midday the reading went on, and the witnesses weigh both the length of it and the rapt attention it commanded. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "from the morning" as "from daylight," and infers that the book of the law must have been a comprehensive one, since out of it Ezra and his companions read hour after hour, selecting appropriate passages; the statement that the ears of all the people were toward the book he takes as a general summary, the detail of which the following verses supply. The reformed John Gill agrees that Ezra did not read straight through in order but selected here and there such passages as it was necessary the people should know.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the span at about six hours, "from the light till mid-day," yet insist it was not one unbroken recitation; the reading went forward alternately with instructive lectures on the law from the Levites, so that hearing and exposition were woven together through the whole morning. And "the ears of all the people were directed to the law" — that is, they listened attentively, the same understanding hearers named in the verse before.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on that attention as the heart of the verse. Reading the scriptures in a religious assembly, he says, is an ordinance of God by which he is honoured and his church edified; and on special occasions we must be willing to attend for many hours together on the reading and expounding of the word — those here were thus employed for six hours. The ears of all the people, he marvels, were unto the book of the law, even chained to it; they heard readily and minded every word, for the word of God commands attention and deserves it. If through carelessness we let much slip in the hearing, he warns, there is danger that through forgetfulness we shall let all slip after hearing.

The witnesses do not divide. Whether they measure the hours, note the selective reading, or press the duty of patient attention, they render one portrait: a whole people standing for the better part of a day, their ears fastened upon the long-silent book, so hungry for the word that six hours in the open street seemed no burden but a feast. The very attentiveness that Ellicott calls a general statement Henry turns into a rebuke of every careless hearer, and Keil and Delitzsch into a picture of reading and teaching joined — the very pattern the next verses will unfold in fuller detail.
4:
For the reading a special structure had been raised, and the witnesses attend to this first pulpit and the men who flanked it. The reformed John Gill observes that the Hebrew calls it a "tower," so named for its height and form and for its largeness, since it was built broad enough to hold fourteen men; he compares the pulpit of wood once made for the king to read the law from, and notes that the reading-desks of the later synagogues bore the very same name, as Aben Ezra records. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the novelty: this migdal, a tower or raised platform, is the first intimation in scripture of a pulpit, made to lift the reader high enough for all to see and hear him, for the next verse says he was above all the people. Yet Clarke cannot resist a jibe at his own day — it was nothing like those tubs or barrels ridiculously set up in churches, in which a preacher is nearly as confined as if he were in the stocks.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the details. Keil and Delitzsch describe a raised stage of wood made for the purpose, with six men standing on Ezra's right hand and seven on his left; they note that the parallel in the Greek Esdras lists seven on the left as well, inserting the name Azariah, which they judge to have dropped from the Hebrew text by a clerical slip, since it is unlikely one side held fewer than the other. They venture cautiously to connect some of these names — Urijah perhaps the father of the Meremoth of Neh. 3:4, and others met again in the building lists. Charles Ellicott agrees that the word is literally "a tower of wood," and that fourteen persons in all stood with Ezra on what is afterwards called a platform or stair beside him.

The witnesses do not divide. They render a single vivid scene: a wooden tower thrown up in the street for the occasion, Ezra raised upon it in the sight of the whole congregation, and a double row of Levites ranged to his right and left — whether as fellow-readers to relieve him, or as assessors whose presence lent authority and honour to the word. What Gill traces back to the king's platform and forward to the synagogue desk, and what Clarke hails as the birth of the pulpit, all serves the one end the verse means to secure: that the man who held the book should be seen and heard by all, and the law of God read from a height where none could miss it.
5:
The simple act of opening the book becomes, in the witnesses' reading, a moment charged with reverence. The reformed John Gill notes that Ezra was so placed that all could plainly see what he did and the more easily hear him, the pulpit having been made for that very purpose. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark that Ezra, standing on the raised platform, was literally "above all the people," so that when he opened the book it was in the sight of them all, and at that sign the whole congregation rose to its feet. They add a careful caution against the Rabbinic claim that standing at the reading of the law had been an Israelite custom from the days of Moses: it cannot be shown from the Old Testament, they say, that any such rule obtained.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the people's rising as an act of pure respect for the sacred word, and finds in it the origin of a Christian usage still kept: in imitation of this, when the gospel for the day is read in the churches, all the people stand up. The gesture, small in itself, he takes as a standing confession of the honour due to scripture.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose fuller comment gathers these verses together, dwells on the solemnity of the opening. Ezra brought the book forth, he says, with a sense of the great mercy of God in giving them that book, and opened it with a sense of the mercy of being allowed to read it — that it was no longer a spring shut up and a fountain sealed. Henry would have us learn to address ourselves to the services of religion with solemn stops and pauses, and not to go about them rashly: let us consider what we are doing when we take God's book into our hands and open it, and do it deliberately, after the counsel of Eccl. 5:1. When Ezra opened the book all the people stood up, showing respect both to the reader and to the word he was about to read; for it becomes servants to stand when their master speaks to them.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the rising of the whole assembly at the mere opening of the scroll was the outward sign of an inward reverence — the people owning, before a word was read, that what lay open before them was the very word of their God. Whether Keil and Delitzsch guard the history of the custom or Clarke and Henry press its devotion, all see in the standing congregation a rebuke to every careless approach to the holy things of God.
6:
Before a line of the law is expounded, Ezra turns the assembly first toward God in blessing, and the witnesses gather around this opening act of worship. The reformed John Gill explains that Ezra, before reading, addressed God in a short benedictory prayer, ascribing blessing and honour and glory to him and celebrating his greatness as the author and giver of the law — the more fittingly, that what he read might come with greater weight upon those who heard it. He recalls from Maimonides the custom of the synagogue, where the reader, having opened the book, pronounces a blessing — "Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, who hath chosen us out of all people and hath given us his law" — to which all the people answer Amen, as they did here.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch suppose the blessing was perhaps a sentence of thanksgiving such as David used in 1 Chron. 29:10, though scarcely a whole psalm like that of 1 Chron. 16:8; to it the people answered "Amen, Amen," as in 1 Chron. 16:36, lifting up their hands and then bowing down and worshipping the LORD with their faces to the ground. Charles Ellicott traces the same double movement of the body: at Ezra's request the multitude arose, and after his doxology uttered a twofold Amen with lifted hands in token of their fervent assent, and then bowed their faces to the ground in token of adoration. He notes a small point of authorship — that "the great God" is the narrator Nehemiah's phrase, not necessarily Ezra's own, and that the actual words of the blessing are nowhere reported.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the pattern of how a people should come to the word. Ezra was here the people's mouth to God, and they affectionately joined with him: he blessed the LORD as the great God, giving honour to his perfections; and the people, to show their concurrence in both prayer and praise, said Amen, Amen, lifted their hands in token of their desire toward God and their expectation from him, and bowed their heads in reverence and subjection. Thus, Henry urges, must we adore God and address ourselves to him whenever we go to read and hear his word, as those who see God in his word to be very great and very good. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds here too a Christian echo, the church's own "Glory be to God for his holy Gospel," sealed with its Amen. The witnesses do not divide: reading is prefaced by blessing, and the people meet the opened book with lifted hands and bowed faces.
7:
The work of the day was not reading only but understanding, and this verse names the Levites who moved among the people to open the sense of what was read. The reformed John Gill takes the thirteen men listed, and the "Levites" joined to them, to be all of one order — Levites appointed to teach — unless some were priests distinguished from the rest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press the same point of grammar: the named men are themselves Levites, so the copula before "the Levites" must have crept in by a clerical error; several of them — Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Hodijah — appear again among the Levites of Neh. 9:4. Their office, expressed by a verb meaning to cause to understand, was to instruct the people by expounding the law.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley opens out what that instruction involved on two fronts at once. It meant, first, the words: the law was in Hebrew, which the people, having lost much of their language along with their religion during the captivity, now needed rendered into the Chaldee or Syriac that had become their common tongue. And it meant, second, the sense: the Levites expounded the mind and will of God in what they read and applied it to the people's present condition. Wesley reads "the people stood in their place" of the several stations into which so vast a congregation must have been divided for convenience of hearing, since one voice could not reach them all; the Levites, like Ezra on his pulpit, seem to have had their own scaffolds, as a comparison with the standing platform of the next chapter suggests.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the picture into a lesson on the ministry of the word. These men, he says, were employed at the same time in places near at hand, to read and expound to those who could not come within hearing of Ezra; and it is a great mercy to a people to be furnished with ministers apt to teach, whose lips should keep knowledge after the charge of the prophet in Mal. 2:7. He notes the composure of the hearers who stood every one in his place, not straying from one teacher to another to compare them, but keeping his post that he might neither disturb another nor be disturbed himself. The witnesses do not divide; they render a whole apparatus of instruction — a chief reader raised on his tower, and a company of Levites dispersed through the crowd to make the reading understood, so that no part of the great assembly should hear an empty sound of words.
8:
Here the manner of the reading is set down in three short strokes — they read distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand — and the witnesses find in them almost a charter for the preaching of the word. The reformed John Gill pictures the labour shared: Ezra began to read and expound, and when he grew weary others relieved him and did the same. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the disputed word rendered "distinctly." The Rabbis, they note, took it of a rendering of the law into the vulgar Chaldee for those who no longer knew ancient Hebrew; but this sense cannot be established from the word itself, and it is more correct to understand a paraphrastic exposition and application of the law rather than a mere recitation by fixed rules. "Gave the sense," they add, means they made the law comprehensible to the hearers.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the verse both ways at once. John Wesley holds that Ezra and his companions successively gave both a translation of the Hebrew words into the Chaldee and an exposition of the things contained in them. Adam Clarke, reflecting on the verse as the very seed of the later custom of preaching from a text, distinguishes its four movements: they read in the book of the law, the proper matter of all preaching; they read distinctly, analysing and dilating the words; they gave the sense, putting weight to it and showing its value and use; and they caused the people to understand the reading, so that they had a mental taste of what was read and knew the will of God. In this, Clarke thinks, lies the origin of the Chaldee paraphrases and, under providence, of expository preaching itself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the two clauses as one: they expounded the obscurer passages, and in doing so naturally translated into the vernacular Aramaic, so that "caused them to understand" simply explains "gave the sense" — they expounded as they read. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the abiding rule: it is required of those who are teachers by office that they explain the word and give the sense of it, for reading is good and preaching good, but expounding brings the reading and the preaching together, making the reading the more intelligible and the preaching the more convincing. The witnesses come near to dividing here, some pressing translation for a people who had lost their tongue and others exposition for a people who had lost the sense; yet they agree in the end that God is honoured not merely when his word is read but when it is understood.
9:
The reading of the law breaks the people's hearts, and the leaders must turn their grief into festal joy. The reformed John Gill identifies the Tirshatha simply as the governor, the office once held by Zerubbabel and now by Nehemiah. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain why the people wept: the portion read, undoubtedly drawn from Deuteronomy and other parts of the law, was suited to convict them of their transgressions and of the punishments they had incurred, and it made so powerful an impression on the assembled crowds that they mourned and wept — moving Nehemiah, Ezra, and the teaching Levites to still them, since the day, the new moon of the seventh month, was holy to the LORD.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the scene as law and gospel together. The law works death and speaks terror, showing men their sin and misery and thundering its curse; therefore when they heard it they all wept, and it was a good sign that their hearts were tender, like Josiah's when he heard the words of the law. Yet they must not yield unduly to that mourning, for the day was a solemn feast on which it was their duty to rejoice; even sorrow for sin must not hinder our joy in God, but rather lead us to it. Henry marks that Nehemiah is brought into the chapter only now, taking notice of the people's weeping, and that Ezra, though pleased to see them so affected, concurred that the mourning was for the moment unseasonable. Everything is beautiful in its season: as we must not be merry when God calls to mourning, so we must not afflict ourselves when God gives us cause to rejoice.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts it beyond doubt that where the Tirshatha is named Nehemiah himself is meant, this being the title of his office; and he reads the command not to weep as fitting a holy day appointed for general rejoicing in the God who had turned their captivity, restored the law, and re-established his ordinances among them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a note of proportion: the days of high festival were unsuited to public, objective sorrow, for which the coming day of atonement, and the special day of fasting and covenant already in the plan of Nehemiah and Ezra, would give their proper room. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the tears were right and the tenderness a mercy, but that the feast of trumpets was no day to afflict the soul — a time rather to let holy sorrow give way, in its season, to the holy joy the leaders now press upon them.
10:
The remedy for the people's weeping is a feast that reaches beyond themselves, and the witnesses dwell on both its bounty and its ground. The reformed John Gill hears the governor Nehemiah bid them go and enjoy the day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the fare precisely: the "fat" is fat pieces of meat, not rich cakes, and the "sweet" is sweetened drink, the good food and drink of a feast-day such as the banquet of Isa. 25:6; and the "portions" are gifts of food sent to the poor who had prepared nothing, that they too might rejoice — the very custom of sending shares that appears in Esth. 9:22 and 1 Sam. 1:4. The command, they note, folds the needy into the joy.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enlarges the charity: eat and drink the best you have, but while feeding yourselves in the fear of the Lord remember those who cannot feast, and send portions to them, that the joy and thanksgiving may be general and the poor have reason to rejoice as well. This, he insists, is no gluttonous or drunken festival that enervates the body; rather, religious joy, tempered with continual dependence on God, meekness, and self-diffidence, is a powerful means of strengthening the soul, so that every duty becomes both practicable and delightful — a cheerful heart being not only a continual feast but a continual medicine. John Wesley reads the whole to the same end: feast before the Lord and relieve the poor brethren, for the day is holy, the beginning of a joyful month; and the joy of serving God with cheerfulness and thankfulness will give that strength of mind and body they greatly need, both to perform their duties and to withstand their enemies.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers on the great closing sentence, "the joy of the LORD is your strength," which he renders literally "delight in Jehovah is a strong refuge" — a saying, he says, capable of unlimited application in preaching and devotion. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had drawn out its uses: this holy joy, and not a carnal or sensual mirth, arises from an interest in the favour of God, and it is strength — strength for the other duties of the feast, oil to the wheels of obedience, and armour against the spiritual enemies who plot against them, putting the mouth out of taste for the pleasures with which the tempter baits his hooks. The witnesses do not divide; they turn a mourning people toward a joy that feeds the hungry and fortifies the soul.
11:
The command to rejoice must be carried through the crowd, and it falls again to the Levites to quiet the weeping people. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that the Levites made the people quiet and easy, their word carrying the more weight because it was backed by the governor's own authority. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render their appeal — "Hold your peace, that is, give over weeping, for the day is holy; neither be ye grieved" — and mark that the Levites strove to pacify a congregation still overcome, moving among them and repeating the charge until the emotion was mastered and the people gave heed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the same difficulty from the pastor's side: as before, what Ezra spoke from the pulpit was relayed by the Levites in every direction through the multitude, and yet, he observes, there was evidently an almost irrepressible emotion — a grief so deep that it could scarcely be checked even by the assurance that the day was holy. The stilling of it took the concerted effort of the whole company of teachers, passing the word from rank to rank.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very repetition of the charge — first from Nehemiah and Ezra in the verse before, now from the Levites, and each time on the same ground, "the day is holy" — becomes eloquent of how tender the people's conscience had grown under the word. There is a quiet lesson in the scene: that holy mourning is good, but that it must yield in its season to holy joy, and that the same ministers who had wounded the people with the law now labour to bind up the wound and turn them to gladness. The weeping was not rebuked as sin but gently overruled as unseasonable; the Levites do not silence a false grief but redirect a true one, teaching the congregation that the God whose law had just convicted them is the very God in whom they are now bidden to rejoice. It is the office of the faithful teacher both to break and to heal — to read the words that make a people weep, and then to still that weeping with the reminder of the day's own holiness. Here, backed by the governor and moving through the crowd, the Levites do exactly that, until the sound of mourning gives way, in the next verse, to the great mirth of a people comforted.
12:
The leaders' comfort takes hold, and the people turn from tears to a joy that the witnesses are careful to ground rightly. The reformed John Gill notes simply that they went their way to eat and drink freely and cheerfully. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the dispersal: the address of Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites had its effect, and the people went off, some to their houses and some to their lodgings, to keep festal repasts and celebrate the day with joy, because they had taken to heart the words that were declared to them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the sense of that last clause: they "had understood," that is, they had caught the meaning of the very command to rejoice, and obeyed it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a small study in the order of the affections. We ought, he says, to have such command over every passion that, however it breaks out, it may be soon restrained and called in again when we are convinced it is unseasonable; he that rules his own spirit so is better than the mighty. And he marks the sequence with delight: after they had wept, they rejoiced, for holy mourning makes way for holy mirth, and those that sow in tears shall reap in joy — those who tremble at the convictions of the word may triumph in its consolations.

But Henry presses hardest on the ground of the joy. They made great mirth, he observes, not because they had the fat to eat and the sweet to drink and good company, but because they had understood the words that were declared to them. To have the holy scriptures, and helps to understand them, is a very great mercy in which we have abundant reason to rejoice — Bibles and ministers, he says, are the joy of God's Israel. The better we understand the word of God, the more comfort we find in it, for the darkness of trouble arises from the darkness of ignorance and mistake; when the words were first declared the people wept, but when they understood them they rejoiced, finding at last the precious promises made to those who repent and reform, and that there was hope in Israel. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that this was no carnal merriment but a joy born of understanding, the proper fruit of a word at last not only read but grasped.
13:
The feast of trumpets over, the leaders come back the very next day, hungry for more of the word, and the witnesses read their return as a mark of true appetite. The reformed John Gill sets the day: the second of the month and of the new year, the day after the feast of blowing of trumpets, once the law had been read and explained. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note who gathered now — the heads of the houses of all the people, with the priests and Levites, coming to Ezra "to attend to" the words of the law; the phrase, they say, expresses taking an attentive interest, a desire to be further and more deeply instructed by him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that this was not the vast multitude of the first day, since the great feast was not yet come, but the chiefs, who came "to consider," to learn the full meaning of an almost forgotten festival — for the dwelling in booths had fallen into disuse.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley finds a particular grace in the Levites' presence among the learners: they chose rather to confess their ignorance than vainly pretend to more knowledge than they had, showing both humility and serious godliness in being more careful to learn their duty than to preserve their reputation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson. The people had spent the greater part of one day in praying and hearing, and yet, so far from being weary, the chief of them came together the next day, though it was no festival, to hear Ezra expound — which they found more delightful and gainful than any worldly pleasure or profit. The more we converse with the word of God, Henry says, if we rightly understand it and are affected with it, the more we shall covet to converse with it and increase our acquaintance with it, crying, How sweet are thy words unto my mouth; those that understand the scriptures well will still desire to understand them better. He marks too a reversal of place: on the first day Ezra's humility had set the priests and Levites at his right hand and left as teachers with him, but now, made more sensible of their own deficiencies, they sit at his feet as learners — for those who would teach others must themselves first receive instruction, drawing on the wisdom of God that was in Ezra's hand after the pattern of Ezra 7:25. The witnesses do not divide; they honour a leadership that came not to display its knowledge but to deepen it.
14:
Searching the law, the leaders come upon a long-neglected command, and the witnesses mark both the discovery and its meaning. The reformed John Gill notes that whether by hearing the law read the day before or by conversation with Ezra, they perceived that it was enjoined — the precept of the feast of tabernacles set down in Lev. 23:34. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are careful about the manner of the finding. It is not that the heads of the people, a fortnight before the feast, deliberately searched the law to prepare for it; rather, having again betaken themselves to Ezra on the second day for instruction, they met with the precept in the course of reading, and were thereby moved to celebrate the approaching festival in booths as the law directed, publishing the proclamation in all their cities and in Jerusalem.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the feast and its fitness. This was the feast of tabernacles, held in commemoration of their fathers' sojourning in the wilderness after the deliverance from Egyptian bondage; and now, having been just delivered from the Babylonish captivity, and the proper season of the year recurring, it was their especial duty to keep the same feast. The parallel is more than a coincidence of the calendar: a people newly brought home from exile were to re-enact the tent-life of a people newly brought out of slavery.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lesson of the discovery itself. Those that diligently search the scriptures, he says, will find things written there which they had forgotten or not duly considered; and it is a mark of a teachable heart that, when what appears to be our duty is revived after it has been neglected, we set about it at once. The feast of tabernacles was a memorial of Israel's dwelling in tents in the wilderness, a representation of our own tabernacle state in this world, and a type of the holy joy of the gospel church — indeed the conversion of the nations to the faith of Christ is foretold under its figure in Zech. 14:16, where all shall come up to keep the feast of tabernacles, as having here no continuing city. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the command was found rather than sought, that its recovery bound the return from Babylon to the exodus from Egypt, and that a people who had let the ordinance lapse showed the health of their repentance by hastening to obey it.
15:
The proclamation goes out through the cities, and the witnesses attend to the summons and the branches it names. The reformed John Gill reads the verse with Jarchi's help, supplying the sense that the people were to publish abroad the call to keep the feast. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the proclamation in full: they were to go forth to the mount and fetch olive branches, and pine, myrtle, and palm, and branches of thick trees, to make booths as it was written; and, as the following verses show, the people went out and did so, making themselves booths on their roofs and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God and in the open streets.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a difficulty in the wording. There is no such command in Leviticus as the verse seems to quote; the Septuagint inserts "And Ezra spake," but it is better to adopt Houbigant's slight emendation, which reads, "And when they heard it, they proclaimed." The instruction, then, was to go out to the Mount of Olives and gather not precisely the branches the ancient law had required, but such as circumstances allowed — a practical adaptation of the letter to what was at hand. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley identifies the mount as the Mount of Olives, nearest Jerusalem and well stored with olive branches and probably the rest, the trees seeming to have been planted thereabouts chiefly for the use of the city in this very feast, which, though long neglected, ought to have been kept every year; and he takes the place as put by way of eminence for any spot near the several cities of Judah where such branches might be had.

The witnesses do not divide, though they differ over how closely the proclamation follows the letter of Moses. What Keil and Delitzsch take as a faithful publishing of the written precept, Ellicott reads through a textual correction and a pastoral liberty, and Wesley through the geography of a hillside planted for the purpose. All agree on the substance: a people who had rediscovered the command now spread it through every town, sending their households out to strip the boughs from the hills and to build, from olive and myrtle and palm, the booths in which their fathers' wilderness years were to be remembered. The gathering of branches becomes the visible sign of a law found again and at once obeyed.
16:
The proclamation bears fruit at once as the whole city turns out to build, and the witnesses note where the booths rose. The reformed John Gill pictures the people going out of Jerusalem to the mountains near at hand and fetching in the branches of one tree or another to raise their shelters. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses over the housetops named in the verse, recalling that the houses of the East were generally built with flat roofs, on which the people reposed, took the air in the summer heat, and often slept — so that a booth set upon the roof was no strange perch but a familiar place made festal. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott distributes the booths through the city: not only on the roofs but in the internal courtyards of the houses; and in the courts of the house of God, where the ministers of the temple made theirs; while the strangers who had come up to Jerusalem, having no house of their own, built them in the streets and open spaces near the gates.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very spread of the booths becomes a picture worth pausing on. From the flat roofs of private houses to the courts of the temple, from the enclosed yards to the broad street of the water gate and the street of the gate of Ephraim, the little green shelters sprang up everywhere, until the whole city was turned into a wilderness encampment. There was no corner of Jerusalem, high or low, native or stranger's, that did not own the command: the priest built within the sacred courts, the citizen upon his own roof or in his yard, and the homeless pilgrim in the open places by the gates, so that every rank kept the same feast in the same fashion.

What Gill traces to the branches carried down from the hills, and Clarke to the everyday roofs turned to holy use, and Ellicott to every available space claimed for the booths, all speaks of a people so eager to obey the recovered law that they filled their city with the tokens of it. The dwelling in tents that Israel had once done from necessity in the desert, this generation now did from gladness in the streets of the restored capital — the sign of a return home re-enacting the memory of a journey out, and the whole of Jerusalem, roof and court and street alike, confessing the word its fathers had let fall.
17:
The keeping of the feast reaches a height unmatched for centuries, and the witnesses measure both its scale and its joy. The reformed John Gill notes that all who had come again out of the captivity came up to Jerusalem and made their booths there, since it was there alone that the feast was to be kept. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears a deliberate pathos in the title "the children of the captivity," and is careful about the great claim that follows: though the feast of tabernacles had been kept before — under Solomon in 1 Kings 8, and again at the return in Ezra 3:4 — it had never been kept thus, with the whole people universally dwelling in booths. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same "done so" of the manner and the circumstances: they had never kept the feast so joyfully, having not only their old causes of rejoicing but special new ones, nor ever so solemnly and religiously; for whereas of old only the first and last days were held with a holy convocation, now the people assembled and attended the reading of the law on every day of the feast.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that no feast of tabernacles since Joshua's time had been so heartily and piously celebrated, and takes occasion to dismiss the later legend, told in the books of the Maccabees, of a sacred fire hidden in a dry well and rekindled from its mud upon the altar, as worthy of no credit.

That the feast had not been so kept since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun draws the witnesses to a common wonder. It was not that the ordinance had lain wholly untouched through all those generations — Gill and Ellicott both allow that it had been observed at intervals — but that never since the first entry into Canaan under Joshua had the nation as a whole gone out to dwell in booths with this fulness and this gladness. The parallel is exact and moving: as Israel newly settled in the land had once kept it, so Israel newly re-settled after exile keeps it again, and the long silence between only sharpens the joy of the recovery. The witnesses do not divide. They render a people restored to their land and to their law at once, and a "very great gladness" that Scripture itself pauses to record.
18:
The feast closes as it had been kept, with the word of God read through every day of it, and the witnesses attend to that daily reading and the assembly that crowned it. The reformed John Gill takes Ezra to be the reader who went on day by day through the book of the law, from the first day to the last — a thing the more notable, he observes, since only the first and last days were properly the holy convocations. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch leave the subject of the verb indefinite, "he read," without naming Ezra, and set the practice in its legal frame: the reading of the law at the feast of tabernacles was expressly ordered only for the year of release, according to Deut. 31:10, so that this daily reading either fell in such a sabbatical year or went beyond the strict letter in devotion. They fix "the last day" as the seventh, for the eighth, being a solemn assembly, did not belong to the feast of tabernacles proper, as the law of Lev. 23:36 distinguishes.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the closing phrase "according unto the manner" of that same eighth-day assembly, the Azereth or supplementary feast day appointed in Lev. 23:36, kept as the ordinance required.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, gathering the whole solemnity, dwells on the people's perseverance in the word through all the days of the feast. They improved their leisure for this good work, he says, and spare hours cannot be better spent than in studying the scriptures and conversing with them; whether or not this was the year of release in which the law was to be read, they spent all the days of the feast in that good employment. And on the eighth day was the solemn assembly God had appointed, in which they finished the solemnity on the twenty-second of the month — yet did not wholly separate, for the twenty-fourth was set apart for fasting and prayer; holy joy, Henry notes, need no more indispose us for godly sorrow than godly sorrow for holy joy. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the mark of this feast was the word read daily from first to last, a whole people who, having found the book, would not now let a day of the festival pass without it — and who moved from the gladness of the booths toward the humbling of the fast with no jar between the two, each holy in its season.
